Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Dark, water-soaked spots on leaves that later turn brown with a yellow halo; spots on fruit are raised and corky; severe infection causes leaf drop and defoliation.
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria (Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria), favoured by warm, humid, wet weather and spread by splashing water.
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Remove and destroy infected plants; apply copper-based bactericides or streptomycin-containing sprays early; avoid working in wet foliage.
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed/seedlings, rotate crops 2-3 years, practise drip irrigation, and plant resistant varieties.

Pepper__bell___healthy.symptoms: None. Leaves are uniform green with no spots, wilting, mosaics or pest damage.
Pepper__bell___healthy.cause: None. Plant is free from disease and pests.
Pepper__bell___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine care: adequate water, balanced fertiliser and pest scouting.
Pepper__bell___healthy.prevention: Maintain good sanitation, crop rotation and balanced nutrition to keep plants vigorous.

Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Brown to black concentric-ring lesions (target-board appearance) on older lower leaves; yellowing around lesions; leaves dry out and die early.
Potato___Early_blight.cause: Fungus Alternaria solani, favoured by warm temperatures, high humidity and stressed/aging plants.
Potato___Early_blight.treatment: Apply protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) at first sign; remove infected foliage; keep tubers well irrigated to avoid stress.
Potato___Early_blight.prevention: Rotate crops 2-3 years, avoid overhead irrigation, remove plant debris, and use resistant varieties.

Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked grey-green spots that turn dark brown/black with a pale halo; white fuzzy growth on underside in humid conditions; tubers develop brown rotted areas.
Potato___Late_blight.cause: Oomycete Phytophthora infestans, the cause of the Irish potato famine; spreads extremely fast in cool, wet weather.
Potato___Late_blight.treatment: Act fast: apply systemic+contact fungicides (mancozeb + metalaxyl/mefenoxam); destroy infected plants to stop spore spread; harvest and dispose diseased tubers.
Potato___Late_blight.prevention: Use certified seed, resistant varieties, destroy cull piles and volunteer plants, and apply preventive fungicide programmes in wet seasons.

Potato___healthy.symptoms: None. Leaves uniform green with no lesions, necrosis, wilting or fungal growth.
Potato___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Maintain watering, fertilisation and routine scouting.
Potato___healthy.prevention: Crop rotation, certified seed, balanced nutrition and timely irrigation.

Tomato_Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small dark water-soaked spots on leaves, stems and fruit; leaf spots may form yellow halos and enlarge; heavy infection causes leaf drop and spots on green fruit.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria Xanthomonas spp., spread by water splash, wind-driven rain and contaminated tools.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.treatment: Spray copper-based bactericides early; remove severely infected plants; avoid overhead watering.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.prevention: Disease-free seed, crop rotation, drip irrigation, sanitation of stakes and tools, resistant varieties.

Tomato_Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown spots with characteristic concentric rings (bull's-eye pattern) on lower leaves; oldest leaves yellow and die first; stems and fruit may develop lesions.
Tomato_Early_blight.cause: Fungus Alternaria solani, thrives in warm, humid conditions and on stressed or nutrient-deficient plants.
Tomato_Early_blight.treatment: Remove infected lower leaves; apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, copper) preventatively or at first symptoms; apply mulch to reduce splash.
Tomato_Early_blight.prevention: Rotate crops, avoid overhead irrigation, stake/prune for airflow, and maintain balanced fertilisation.

Tomato_Late_blight.symptoms: Large greasy olive-green or grey water-soaked lesions on leaves; white mould on leaf undersides in humid weather; dark firm lesions on stems and fruit; rapid plant collapse.
Tomato_Late_blight.cause: Oomycete Phytophthora infestans, highly destructive; favoured by cool nights, warm days and high moisture.
Tomato_Late_blight.treatment: Destroy infected plants immediately to prevent spread; apply fungicides (copper, mancozeb, chlorothalonil) aggressively; do not compost infected material.
Tomato_Late_blight.prevention: Resistant varieties, crop rotation, avoid overhead irrigation, good airflow, and preventive fungicide schedule in wet seasons.

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale yellow-green spots on upper leaf surface; fluffy olive-brown to purplish mould on the lower surface; leaves curl, wither and drop; mainly affects greenhouse tomatoes.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.cause: Fungus Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum), favoured by high humidity (85%+) and poor ventilation.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.treatment: Improve airflow and reduce humidity; apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, copper); remove infected leaves.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.prevention: Space plants wider, prune for ventilation, water at base, manage greenhouse humidity, use resistant cultivars.

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Numerous small circular spots with grey-tan centres and dark brown rims on oldest leaves; leaves yellow, then brown and drop; works upward from the bottom.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Fungus Septoria lycopersici, spread by rain splash; renders plants weak and reduces yield when defoliation is severe.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.treatment: Remove infected lower leaves and debris; apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper sprays; stake and mulch to reduce splash.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.prevention: Crop rotation (avoid solanaceous hosts), overhead-water avoidance, removal of debris, resistant varieties.

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.symptoms: Fine yellow-white stippling/speckling on leaves; fine webbing on undersides and between stems; leaves bronze, dry and drop; mites are tiny moving dots, worse in hot dry weather.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.cause: Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae), a tiny arachnid pest that multiplies rapidly in heat and drought.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.treatment: Wash plants with water to knock mites down; apply miticides (abamectin, spiromesifen) or insecticidal soap/neem; release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis).
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.prevention: Maintain humidity, avoid drought stress, inspect undersides regularly, control weeds that host mites.

Tomato__Target_Spot.symptoms: Circular necrotic spots with distinct concentric rings (target-like) on leaves, stems and fruit; fruit spots can be sunken with dark halos; severe leaf drop in wet conditions.
Tomato__Target_Spot.cause: Fungus Corynespora cassiicola, favoured by warm temperature and high humidity with prolonged leaf wetness.
Tomato__Target_Spot.treatment: Apply fungicides (azoxystrobin, chlorothalonil, mancozeb) at first symptoms; improve airflow and remove infected debris.
Tomato__Target_Spot.prevention: Resistant/tolerant varieties, drip irrigation, crop rotation, avoid dense planting, preventive fungicide in high-risk weather.

Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mottled light-and-dark green mosaic pattern on leaves; leaves may crinkle, curl or become fern-like; stunted growth and reduced fruit set; fruits may show uneven ripening.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Tomato mosaic virus, transmitted mechanically via hands, tools, and contaminated seed/clothing (not by insects).
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.treatment: No cure; remove and destroy infected plants; disinfect hands and tools with milk or bleach solution; do not replant solanaceous crops immediately.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.prevention: Use virus-free seed, disinfect tools/benches, avoid touching plants when wet, control weeds, use resistant cultivars.

Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.symptoms: Leaves curl upward and inward, yellowing at edges and between veins; plants severely stunted; few or no flowers/fruits; spread by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci).
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.cause: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, a begomovirus transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.treatment: No cure for infected plants; remove and destroy affected plants; control the whitefly vector with yellow sticky traps and targeted insecticides.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.prevention: Protect seedlings with insect netting, use resistant varieties, control whiteflies early, remove alternate weed hosts, rogue infected plants promptly.

Tomato_healthy.symptoms: None. Uniform green leaves without spots, discolouration, curling, mould or pest damage.
Tomato_healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Continue regular watering, fertilisation and monitoring.
Tomato_healthy.prevention: Good sanitation, rotation, balanced feeding, proper spacing and routine scouting.
